rationale: Otto and colleagues originally measured serum S100 in patients referred for suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and compared findings with other diagnoses and controls. Table 5 lists one Parkinson case among the differential diagnoses and reports a biomarker value. Back pain appears as a separate diagnostic entry in that table. Methods and results do not compare dried date fruit consumption or measure its effect on pain severity.

The investigators followed a clinical series initially referred with medically unexplained motor symptoms and reassessed neurological and psychiatric diagnoses. The observations include pain as a reported symptom. Data collection and adjusted analyses compare clinical histories and outcomes without date fruit as an assigned or measured dietary exposure.

Eleven expedition members crossed over between temazepam and placebo at Everest base camp. The printed methods describe allocation and overnight oximetry. The results compare subjective sleep and oxygen desaturation. The word falls in the table denotes drops in arterial oxygen saturation. No date fruit intervention or Parkinson pain assessment was described.

The study compares oral contraceptive use and inherited prothrombotic factors between women with cerebral sinus thrombosis and population controls. The results and table compare medication exposure and thrombosis risk. They supply no dietary date fruit variable or Parkinson pain severity comparison.

The two published case narratives use cerebral perfusion imaging alongside clinical follow-up and postmortem diagnosis. Fatigue, rigidity and mood changes are part of the neurological histories. Neither case has studied date fruit consumption or a measured pain response after it.

The study groups middle-aged men by questionnaire-derived alcohol intake and compares plasma lipoprotein concentrations. The Methods identify alcohol questionnaire fields and laboratory endpoints. Dietary date fruit and Parkinson pain severity are absent from the comparison.
